name: Freya Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Freya, thanks for doing this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything here is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you describe a normal working day for me?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the live-line team at our electricity co-operative, which covers a big patch of lakes and forest. Live-line means we work on the wires while they're still carrying power, so the farms and the dairy don't lose supply, using long insulated poles we call hot sticks, or gloves and a bucket truck with a lot of rubber between you and the ground. Before we roll out, I've already had the AI on my laptop turn last night's drone pictures into a list of hot joints and cracked insulators, and I check its list against my own eyes over coffee. Then it's out on the gravel roads, usually two or three jobs a day.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you love about it, and what grinds you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the concentration. When you're working a live line, the whole world shrinks to your hands and the conductor, and you can't think about your tax return. What grinds me down is the driving and the cold, and the fact that I'm the only woman on the team over fifty and I still get asked if I need help lifting things. Last year I volunteered to trial a robotic arm on one of the trucks, and the others thought I'd gone mad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, honestly, that's a bit of a shame. Online I'd post something like, well, back to doing it the hard way. At work the lads would tease me for weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I finish my career the way I started it, which is fine but a bit dull. I was looking forward to teaching a robot to hold the hot stick while I drank my coffee. I'm only half joking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I do. I'd still use the AI for the drone reports and the job plans, because it already saves me an hour a day. I'd keep my savings ticking over and keep planning to retire at sixty-two and maybe teach at the training centre part-time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, slightly disappointed. Like when the new bridge they promised you gets cancelled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You volunteered for the robot arm. How did that trial go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half good. The arm held the conductor steady, which saved my shoulders, but it was slow and it didn't like the cold. We had to warm its battery in the truck cab like a puppy. I wrote a two-page report on what it needed and the supplier actually read it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you push for more tools even if AI stalled?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, small ones. Better drones, better sensors, the AI for reports. None of it needs a revolution to be useful, it just needs someone who's willing to try it and complain properly when it's rubbish.

S0.say: She'd say it's a bit of a shame and post that it's back to doing things the hard way. Her colleagues would tease her about it for weeks.
S0.think: She thinks it means finishing her career the way she started it, which is fine but a bit dull. She'd been looking forward to robots taking some strain.
S0.do: Keeps using AI for drone reports and job plans, which saves her about an hour a day. Keeps saving steadily and plans to retire at sixty-two and maybe teach part-time at the training centre.
S0.feel: Calm, with mild disappointment, like a promised bridge being cancelled.
S0.quote: I was looking forward to teaching a robot to hold the hot stick while I drank my coffee.
S0.fieldNote: Freya is the rare lineworker who is disappointed when the technology doesn't arrive. She already uses AI daily and volunteered for a robot arm trial, writing detailed feedback to the supplier. Her humour about warming the robot's battery like a puppy shows how hands-on her curiosity is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the good version, as long as we get it right. At work I'd say let's get ahead of it and pick the tools ourselves instead of having them chosen for us. At the union meeting I'd say we need a technology clause in the next contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's mostly good news. I'm curious, I like learning, and I've got the savings to not panic. I'd rather be the woman who trains the robots than the woman who gets replaced by one, and at my age I get to pick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the co-op to make me the lead on the robot and sensor rollout, starting this winter. I'd take the supplier's training course and any short course on robot maintenance going at the technical college. I'd also push the union for a clause saying tasks that go to machines come with retraining, not redundancies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, honestly. With a little guilt for being excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're progressive and you back unions. Isn't it odd to be excited about machines that take tasks away from workers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's not odd to me. Machines that hold heavy conductors mean fewer wrecked shoulders, and I've buried two friends from this job. What's odd is letting the company decide alone what the savings are spent on. I want the robots, and I want the union deciding who benefits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stig, who's fifty-four and hates screens. He's the best climber I've ever seen, but he types with one finger and swears at the tablet. I'd sit with him and show him things slowly, the way someone once showed me how to read a load chart.

S1.say: She'd call it the good version if done right, urging colleagues to pick their own tools rather than have them chosen. At the union she'd ask for a technology clause in the next contract.
S1.think: She thinks it's mostly good news for her, since she's curious, likes learning and has savings. At her age, she gets to choose to train the robots rather than be replaced.
S1.do: Asks the co-operative to make her lead on the robot and sensor rollout starting this winter and takes supplier and college courses on robot maintenance. Pushes the union for a contract clause tying automation to retraining, not redundancies.
S1.feel: Excited, with a little guilt for being excited.
S1.quote: I'd rather be the woman who trains the robots than the woman who gets replaced by one, and at my age I get to pick.
S1.fieldNote: When I named the possible tension between union values and robot enthusiasm, she had a clear answer: robots for safety, union for sharing the gains. She's personally motivated by friends lost on the job. Her plan to sit slowly with a screen-shy colleague shows her progressive values in practice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is far too fast and someone should hit the brakes. At the union I'd say we need a public plan now, not a consultation in eighteen months. Online I'd be a lot less cheerful than usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I'd be okay. I've got savings, the cabin by the lake, and I'm the person at the co-op who already knows how the robots behave, so I'd probably be busier for a while, not out of work. What frightens me isn't the robots, it's two years, because nobody organises anything fair in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to run the robot rollout so at least someone who knows the lines is in charge of it. I'd put some savings into the co-op's members' fund, because if the co-op owns the machines, the money stays local. And I'd be at the union's emergency meeting arguing for income support for the ones who get pushed out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'm safe and I know it, and I don't like watching other people not be safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be sixty in 2028. Would you stay on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably till sixty-two, maybe longer if they needed me to supervise the machines. It would be strange: the robot on the line and me in the truck with a tablet, watching. I think I'd miss the concentration of having my own hands on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the farms and the people the co-op serves?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit I'd lose sleep over, if anything. The dairy, the sawmill, the shop in the village, everyone would be hit at once, and the co-op might be the only thing still standing. I'd want the co-op board to use the savings from the robots to keep prices down for members.

S2.say: She'd say it's far too fast and someone should hit the brakes. She'd push the union for a public plan now and be much less cheerful online than usual.
S2.think: She thinks she'd be okay, with savings, a lake cabin and robot experience that would make her busier for a while. What frightens her is the two-year speed, because nothing fair gets organised that quickly.
S2.do: Volunteers to run the robot rollout at the co-operative so someone who knows the lines is in charge. Puts some savings into the co-op's members' fund to keep ownership local, and argues for income support at an emergency union meeting.
S2.feel: Uneasy: safe and aware of it, and uncomfortable watching others not be safe.
S2.quote: What frightens me isn't the robots, it's two years, because nobody organises anything fair in two years.
S2.fieldNote: Even in the fastest picture her own position looks secure, and she knows it. Her worry is the speed and fairness, and her answer is local ownership through the co-op. She'd miss having her own hands on the line, which was a quieter, more personal admission than her usual enthusiasm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a real window, so use it. At work I'd say every crew should have someone who can run and fix the machines by 2030. I'd post about it, probably too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me this one's close to ideal. I'd get to shape it properly at the co-op and leave on a high. I'd have time to bring the others along instead of just watching them get left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set up a training plan at the co-op, with me teaching the robot side and Stig teaching the old climbing side to the apprentices, so we keep both. I'd get a proper qualification in robot maintenance by 2028. I'd ask the board to put in writing that workers get first pick of the new roles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and quite energised. It feels like a project I'd be good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does three more years change what you'd do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the fast one we'd be scrambling. In this one we'd have time to train people, test the machines on real ice and real storms, and argue about who gets what. Three years is the difference between a fire drill and a fire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change your retirement plan at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe stay a year longer, to sixty-three, to see the rollout through. Pete would grumble, he's already bought fishing gear for both of us. But I think he'd understand.

S3.say: She'd say there's a real window and every crew should have someone able to run and fix the machines by 2030. She'd probably post about it too much.
S3.think: She thinks this picture is close to ideal for her: she'd shape the change at the co-operative and leave on a high. She'd have time to bring colleagues along instead of watching them get left behind.
S3.do: Sets up a co-operative training plan pairing robot skills with traditional climbing skills, and earns a robot maintenance qualification by 2028. Asks the board to guarantee workers first pick of new roles and considers staying a year past sixty-two.
S3.feel: Calm and energised, as if it's a project she'd be good at.
S3.quote: Three years is the difference between a fire drill and a fire.
S3.fieldNote: The five-year picture is close to her ideal: enough time to train people and test machines in real conditions. She'd pair herself with the screen-shy climber to teach both skill sets, keeping the old knowledge alive. Her partner's fishing gear is a nice detail about what she'd be postponing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to get it right, so I'll be very cross if we don't. At the union I'd say this is the moment to win a shorter working week, not lose jobs. I'd say it everywhere, at the shop, at family dinners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I'd be retired before it fully lands, teaching part-time at the training centre. I'd probably teach the robot courses. I'd be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the AI and push the co-op to start robot trials early, so we're not rushed later. I'd plan to retire at sixty-two and then teach two days a week at the training centre on new equipment. I'd vote for whoever promised a shorter week and retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit wistful. I'd quite like to see the end of it from the inside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is ten years too slow for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. I'm the strange one who wants the future to hurry up, and everyone else wants it to wait until they've retired. But ten years means fewer people get hurt, so I'd take it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your sons to know about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the people who did the hard work kept the country running, and the machines should do the same for them. And that they should be curious, not frightened. Both of them are, already, which I'm glad about.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is enough to get it right and this is the moment to win a shorter working week. She'd say it at the shop and at family dinners.
S4.think: She thinks she'd be retired before it fully lands, teaching part-time and probably running the robot courses. She'd be fine.
S4.do: Keeps using AI and pushes the co-operative to start robot trials early to avoid rushing later. Plans to retire at sixty-two and teach two days a week on new equipment at the training centre, voting for whoever backs a shorter week and retraining.
S4.feel: Calm and a bit wistful, wishing she could see it from the inside.
S4.quote: That the people who did the hard work kept the country running, and the machines should do the same for them.
S4.fieldNote: She admits she's an outlier who wants the future to hurry up while others want it delayed. Yet she accepts the ten-year version because it means fewer people get hurt. Her progressive streak shows up as wanting a shorter working week rather than fewer jobs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, not for me but for the village. What would help is a rule that public and co-op utilities keep ownership of the machines, so the savings come back to the members, plus income support that starts the day someone loses their job, not six months later.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether the robots work in the cold. They don't yet, not properly. Somebody needs to test them on a frozen lake road in January before anyone promises the world. I'd happily volunteer.

headlineQuote: I'm the strange one who wants the future to hurry up, and everyone else wants it to wait until they've retired.
portrait: Freya Jensen is a 58-year-old live-line team leader at a rural electricity co-operative who uses AI every day and volunteered to trial a robot arm on her truck. She's progressive and pro-union but sees robots as a way to save workers' bodies, as long as the gains are shared. With savings and a lake cabin, she's calm in most pictures, even a little disappointed by the plateau. The two-year AGI picture makes her uneasy because of the speed and the hit to her village, while the five-year one is close to her ideal: time to train people and shape the rollout before she retires to teach.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture worries her most, not for herself but for her village and the people the co-op serves.
whatWouldHelp: Keeping ownership of the machines with public and co-op utilities so savings come back to members, and income support that starts the day someone loses their job.
